facts.title: Born from a Swedish village
facts.text: Yttrium owes its name to Ytterby, a tiny quarry village near Stockholm, Sweden. In 1787 the chemist Carl Axel Arrhenius found a heavy black mineral there that he called ytterbite, later renamed gadolinite. From this single rock, Johan Gadolin isolated a new "earth" in 1794 — the first identification of yttrium's oxide.

facts.title: One village, four elements
facts.text: Ytterby is the most element-honored place on Earth, lending its name to four elements: yttrium, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium. Three more elements found in the same ore — scandium, holmium, and thulium — were named for Scandinavia and nearby regions. No other location has inspired so many entries on the periodic table.

facts.title: A metal that resists fire
facts.text: Yttrium metal forms a protective oxide film that makes it surprisingly stable in air, even though finely divided shavings can ignite above about 400 degrees Celsius. Bulk yttrium melts at 1526 degrees Celsius and stays solid in air far better than most reactive metals. This durability is why small amounts are added to alloys to improve their resistance to oxidation at high temperature.

facts.title: The red glow in old TVs
facts.text: For decades, yttrium compounds produced the vivid red phosphors in color television tubes and computer monitors. Yttrium oxysulfide and yttrium oxide doped with europium emit a pure, bright red when struck by electrons or ultraviolet light. The same europium-doped yttrium phosphors later helped create the warm tones in compact fluorescent and white LED lighting.

facts.title: A laser crystal workhorse
facts.text: The most famous laser crystal in the world, Nd:YAG, is yttrium aluminum garnet (Y3Al5O12) with a sprinkling of neodymium. These lasers cut and weld metal, perform eye surgery, and remove tattoos, emitting infrared light at 1064 nanometers. Yttrium provides the rigid, transparent crystal lattice that hosts the light-emitting neodymium ions.

facts.title: It made superconductors warm
facts.text: In 1987 researchers created YBCO — yttrium barium copper oxide — which superconducts at 93 kelvin, above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen. This was a landmark, because cheap liquid nitrogen (77 K) could now cool a superconductor instead of costly liquid helium. The discovery earned worldwide attention and remains central to research on magnets, power cables, and levitation.

facts.title: A radioactive cancer fighter
facts.text: The isotope yttrium-90 is a pure beta emitter used in targeted cancer treatment. Tiny radioactive glass or resin microspheres are delivered into the blood vessels feeding liver tumors, where Y-90 destroys cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue. It is also attached to antibodies to treat certain lymphomas, making yttrium a quiet hero of nuclear medicine.

facts.title: Strengthening exotic alloys
facts.text: Adding a small fraction of yttrium dramatically improves high-temperature alloys used in jet engines and gas turbines. It helps the protective oxide layer cling tightly to the metal surface, slowing corrosion in brutal heat. Yttrium is also used to remove sulfur and oxygen impurities from molten metals such as vanadium and chromium.

facts.title: Forged in dying stars
facts.text: Yttrium is not made in the cores of ordinary stars by simple fusion; most of it is built by the slow neutron-capture process in aging red giant stars. Astronomers detect yttrium lines in stellar spectra to trace how heavy elements were cooked across cosmic history. The yttrium in your phone or TV was literally manufactured inside ancient stars before the Sun was born.

facts.title: Common, but never alone
facts.text: Despite its exotic reputation, yttrium is fairly abundant — roughly 30 parts per million in Earth's crust, more common than lead. The catch is that it never occurs as a free metal and is always mixed with the chemically similar rare-earth elements, making separation difficult and expensive. Major sources today include monazite and xenotime sands and ion-adsorption clays mined in southern China.
